title: TypeScript Object Types: Interfaces, Unions and Structural Typing
summary: Quick revision notes on shaping object types in TypeScript: interfaces vs type aliases, optional and readonly properties, unions and intersections, literal types, structural typing and excess property checks.

chapters.title: Object Types Mental Model
points: Structural typing: a value fits a type if it has the required members, regardless of declared name or class
An object type describes required members and their types: { id: number; name: string }
interface and type both name an object shape; the same variable can satisfy either interchangeably
Types are erased at compile time, so no runtime check exists; validate external data separately
Assignability is directional: a wider object (extra members) is assignable to a narrower type, not the reverse

chapters.title: Interfaces vs Type Aliases
points: interface User { id: number } declares an object shape; type User = { id: number } does the same
interface extends another: interface Admin extends User { role: string }; alias uses intersection: type Admin = User & { role: string }
Declaration merging: two interface User blocks merge into one; a duplicate type alias is an error
Only type aliases can name unions, primitives, tuples and mapped or conditional types: type ID = string | number
Rule of thumb: interface for public object and class contracts, type for anything else

chapters.title: Optional and Readonly Properties
points: Optional property: nickname?: string has type string | undefined and may be omitted
Optional is not the same as nullable: { a?: string } allows omission, { a: string | undefined } still requires the key
readonly id: number blocks reassignment: user.id = 2 is a compile error
readonly is shallow: readonly tags: string[] still allows tags.push(); use ReadonlyArray<string> or readonly string[] for contents
readonly is compile-time only; Readonly<T> makes all properties readonly and Partial<T> makes all optional

chapters.title: Unions, Intersections and Literal Types
points: Union A | B: value is one of the types; only members common to all are accessible until you narrow
Narrow unions with typeof, in, instanceof or equality checks inside if or switch
Intersection A & B: value has all members of both; conflicting property types collapse to never
Literal types: type Dir = 'up' | 'down' restricts to exact values; const x = 'up' infers the literal, let x = 'up' widens to string
Discriminated union: a shared literal field (kind: 'circle' | 'square') lets switch narrow each case; add a never default for exhaustiveness checks

chapters.title: Structural Typing and Excess Property Checks
points: Two types with identical structure are interchangeable; different names do not make them incompatible
Excess property check applies only to fresh object literals: const u: User = { id: 1, extra: 2 } errors
Assigning the same object through a variable skips the check: const o = { id: 1, extra: 2 }; const u: User = o is allowed
Bypass or opt in: use a type assertion (as User), or add an index signature [key: string]: unknown to accept extras
Weak type detection: a type with all-optional properties errors if the value shares none of them
Brand a type ({ __brand: 'UserId' } & string) when structurally identical types must not be mixed

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Object Types
points: interface = extendable, mergeable object contract; type = unions, tuples, aliases, mapped types
Optional: prop?: T (T | undefined); readonly prop: T (shallow, compile-time only)
A | B = one of; A & B = all of; discriminate unions with a literal kind field
Literal widening: const keeps literal, let widens; use as const to freeze object literals to literal readonly types
Excess property check: fresh literals only; structural compatibility otherwise
